I have farmed this land in Quzhou for over fifty years. My husband passed away ten years ago, and now my youngest son helps me with the heavy work when he is not working in the county town. I have four mu of good flat land near the well, plus one mu of slightly sandy soil on the edge of the plot. I finished middle school — more than many women my age in the village — so I can read the seed bags and fertilizer labels myself, though I still trust my hands and eyes more than anything written on paper.

This year, I will stick with what I know. On my four mu of good land, I already have winter wheat in the ground. I sowed it last October after rotary tillage, using the same improved lumai variety I have used for years. It is reliable, and the grain station buys it without trouble. I will give it four irrigations — the winter irrigation is already done, and now I need to water at green-up, jointing, and grain-filling. For fertilizer, I will spread my usual compound fertilizer and topdress with urea when the weather warms. I expect about 1000 jin per mu if the spring drought does not get too bad. After harvest in early June, I will plant hybrid maize — probably nongda372 or denghai605, whichever the cooperative has in stock. I never till for maize; I just direct-seed into the wheat stubble the same day we thresh. It saves time and the soil stays moist. Two irrigations for the maize, and three or four pesticide sprays, should be enough.

On my remaining one mu of sandy land, I will plant cotton. The soil is too light for wheat, but cotton does well there, and the price has been steady. I will rotary-till in April and sow the improved guoxinmian seeds. Cotton needs more care — about ten sprays for bollworms and aphids — but my son can help carry the tanks. I have managed cotton since I was a young bride; I know when the leaves turn and when to stop watering before the bolls open.

I am seventy-one. I do not gamble with new crops or fancy techniques. The wheat-maize rotation feeds us and brings sure money. The cotton gives extra cash for medicine and my granddaughter's school fees. That is enough.
